meta.audience: Readers of the abridgment; within the chapter, the people of Limhi at the temple
meta.location: The land of Zarahemla, then the land of Lehi-Nephi and Shilom

world_behind.title: A king moved by nagging
world_behind.text: Verse 1 says the people wearied Mosiah with their teasings until he sent an expedition. The noun appears once in scripture. The whole Zeniff record, eighteen chapters of it, opens because a population would not stop asking.

world_behind.title: Forty days lost
world_behind.text: Sixteen strong men set out not knowing the route and wander forty days. The number is the wilderness number, and the record uses it without comment for a party that is simply lost. Their ancestors had made the same journey in a generation the reader has already read about.

world_behind.title: Three generations in one sentence
world_behind.text: Verse 9 has Limhi introducing himself as son of Noah, son of Zeniff. The reader has not yet been told who any of them are. A dynasty and its decline are compressed into a self-introduction, and the next seventeen chapters unpack it.

world_behind.title: A fifty percent tribute
world_behind.text: Verse 22 itemizes it: half the corn, half the barley, half of all grain, half the increase of flocks and herds, half of everything. Ancient vassal tribute was typically a fraction of that. The number is what makes verse 15's proposal intelligible.

world_behind.title: The exodus recital
world_behind.text: Verse 19 runs a set piece: the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; Israel brought out of Egypt; the Red Sea crossed dry; manna in the wilderness. Israel had a standing form for rehearsing its deliverance, and Limhi uses it on a people who need one.

world_behind.title: Hosea, twice, in two forms
world_behind.text: Verses 30 and 31 give the same oracle in variant wordings: sow filthiness and reap the chaff in the whirlwind; sow filthiness and reap the east wind. Hosea's line is sowing wind and reaping whirlwind. The record preserves both versions consecutively.

world_behind.title: A prophet identified by his doctrine
world_behind.text: Verses 26 through 28 report a chosen man of God killed for teaching that Christ is God and that man was made in his image. He is not named here. The reader meets Abinadi as a teaching before meeting him as a person.

words.text: Fetters: what binds a prisoner, not a group of men. They are loosed in verse 8 and Ammon refers to having worn them in verse 13. The word runs through this whole section of the record, and Limhi's people are about to spend seventeen chapters in a condition it names.

Limhi means it as a charge, demanding to know what made these men "so bold as to come near the walls of the city" (v. 10). Two verses later Ammon takes it up as a virtue and promises to endeavor to speak with boldness. He does not dispute the king's account of what he did. He keeps the word and applies it to what he is about to say.

cites.quote: so bold as to come near the walls of the city

spans.text: so bold as to come near the walls of the city

words.text: Here the verb means to allow. Limhi has suffered the strangers to be preserved rather than killed, Ammon says the king would not have suffered him to wear bands had he known who he was, and the Lord, later in the speech, would not have suffered the great evil to come on a people who had not transgressed. The other sense arrives at verse 16, where men who wandered forty days had suffered hunger, thirst, and fatigue. Both senses are the King James Bible's, and the chapter moves between them within five verses without any signal that the word has changed.

Skill turned to deceit. Limhi uses it of king Laman, whose treaty was the instrument, and pairs it with "cunning." The verse assigns the blame twice over, to Laman's craft and to Zeniff's over-zeal, and does not let either excuse the other.

To marvel, used here in a rhetorical question that expects nobody. Who wondereth that they are in bondage? Limhi has just finished the causal chain and the verb invites his audience to find it unsurprising, a hard thing to ask of people in chains.

The effect named at the end of the first oracle, and the word does not appear in Hosea's version. Chaff in a whirlwind is worthless; poison is actively harmful. The addition turns a saying about futile harvest into one about a harvest that kills.

phrases.term: They wearied him with their teasings
phrases.text: An unheroic reason for an expedition. Persistence. The record is candid that the chain of events producing eighteen chapters of scripture began with people pestering a king until he gave in.

phrases.term: They knew not the course they should travel
phrases.text: Stated plainly before the forty days. The expedition is not divinely guided and the record does not pretend otherwise. What follows is competent men lost in country their own grandparents had crossed.

phrases.term: I am Limhi, the son of Noah, who was the son of Zeniff
phrases.text: A king establishing standing by descent, to strangers, while they stand bound in front of him. The reader is given a lineage before a character, and every name in it will matter. It is the most information-dense sentence in the chapter.

phrases.term: It is better that we be slaves to the Nephites than to pay tribute to the king of the Lamanites
phrases.text: A people proposing their own enslavement as an improvement. Limhi is describing arithmetic: half of everything, or servitude to kin. The sentence is the clearest measure in the record of what the bondage actually cost.

phrases.term: Yet I trust there remaineth an effectual struggle to be made
phrases.text: The phrase occurs once in scripture. Placed immediately after an admission that the previous strugglings were in vain, it distinguishes effort that works from effort that merely happens, and offers hope on the basis of the difference rather than by denying the failures.

phrases.term: That God who was the God of Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob
phrases.text: The title that identifies God by a history. Limhi is arguing from precedent: this is the one who has done this kind of thing before. Everything in the verse after it is evidence. Egypt, the sea, the manna.

phrases.term: He being over-zealous to inherit the land of his fathers
phrases.text: The diagnosis of a grandfather, delivered by a grandson to a nation in chains. The fault named is excess of a good motive. Zeniff will use the same word of himself two chapters later, which makes this the rare case where the record's judgment and the man's own agree.

phrases.term: Even one half of all we have or possess the king of the Lamanites doth exact of us, or our lives
phrases.text: The alternative stated at the end of the clause: half of everything, or your life. Limhi itemizes the grain and the flocks first and puts the choice last, so the sentence reads as an inventory that turns into a threat.

phrases.term: A prophet of the Lord have they slain; yea, a chosen man of God
phrases.text: Reported as a fact of national history, unnamed and undated within the speech. Limhi lists it as the culminating item in a chain of transgression, and it is the hinge of his whole argument about why they are where they are.

phrases.term: He said that man was created after the image of God
phrases.text: The doctrine that got a man killed, restated by the king who inherited the consequences. Genesis says God created man in his own image; Limhi's report runs it the other way. The image man was created after is the one God would take. The killing followed from that inversion.

phrases.term: I will not succor my people in the day of their transgression
phrases.text: Succor is a verb of running to someone's aid, and this is the only place in the record where God says he will not. The withholding is tied to a day rather than to a person, which leaves the sentence temporary by construction.

phrases.term: If my people shall sow filthiness they shall reap the chaff thereof in the whirlwind
phrases.text: Hosea says sow wind, reap whirlwind; this says sow filthiness, reap chaff in a whirlwind, and adds that the effect is poison. Then verse 31 gives the same oracle again with the east wind and immediate destruction. Two forms of one saying, preserved side by side without a word about the difference.

phrases.term: If ye will turn to the Lord with full purpose of heart
phrases.text: The conclusion, and the conditions are three: turn, trust, serve with all diligence of mind. The promise attached is deliverance "according to his own will and pleasure," which withholds the timing in the same breath that it grants the outcome.

verses.label: v. 1–6
verses.title: The expedition
verses.text: Three years of peace, a curiosity nobody will drop, sixteen strong men sent under Ammon, no knowledge of the route, forty days of wandering, a hill north of Shilom, and four men going down into the land. Six verses to get the party into the story, and the only thing that goes right is that they arrive.

verses.label: v. 7–13
verses.title: Arrest and recognition
verses.text: Seized by the king's guard, bound, imprisoned two days, brought out, and commanded to answer. Limhi identifies himself by three generations and demands to know why they came. Ammon bows, thanks God he is alive, and says his name, at which point the whole situation reverses.

verses.label: v. 14–17
verses.title: Relief, and a summons
verses.text: Limhi is exceedingly glad, knows his brethren are alive, will rejoice and make his people rejoice tomorrow; explains the bondage and the tribute; unbinds the prisoners and feeds them; and sends a proclamation for the people to gather at the temple. The second temple assembly in seven chapters.

verses.label: v. 18–20
verses.title: Lift up your heads
verses.text: Comfort, a time at hand, an admission that past strugglings were vain, and the promise of an effectual one. Then the recital (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Egypt, the Red Sea, the manna), and the conclusion: the same God brought our fathers here, and it is our own iniquities that brought the bondage.

verses.label: v. 21–25
verses.title: How it happened
verses.text: Zeniff over-zealous, Laman cunning, a treaty, land yielded, the whole thing designed to produce subjection; then the tribute itemized, the mourning justified, the blood spilt in vain, and the cause named as transgression. Limhi builds a case before he brings the charge.

verses.label: v. 26–28
verses.title: A killing, and its reason
verses.text: A chosen man of God slain for saying that Christ is God, that he would take the image of man, and that man was made after God's image. They killed him, they did much else, and Limhi asks who could be surprised at the result.

verses.label: v. 29–33
verses.title: The oracles, and the way out
verses.text: God will not succor in the day of transgression, will hedge up their ways, will make their own doings a stumbling block; whirlwind and chaff and poison; east wind and immediate destruction; the promise is fulfilled and you are afflicted. And then the condition: turn, trust, serve, and he will deliver, on his own schedule.

chapter.title: The record admits an ignoble beginning
chapter.text: Eighteen chapters of scripture start because a population nagged a king. No revelation sends the expedition, no vision guides it, and the party gets lost for forty days. The narrative that follows is providential in its outcome and entirely ordinary in its opening.

chapter.title: A second temple assembly, and a different sermon
chapter.text: Benjamin gathered a free people to give them a name; Limhi gathers a people in chains to explain why. The two scenes are seven chapters apart, share a location type and a proclamation, and land in opposite circumstances. The arrangement looks deliberate.

chapter.title: The bondage is explained without excusing anyone
chapter.text: Laman's craftiness, Zeniff's over-zeal, the people's contentions, a murdered prophet. Limhi names an external cause and three internal ones and does not let the first carry the weight. The nation's condition is presented as earned.

chapter.title: Abinadi arrives as a doctrine
chapter.text: The reader is told what the prophet taught and why it killed him before being told his name or his story. When the account arrives eight chapters later, the stakes are already established. A compiler arranged it that way.

chapter.title: Two versions of one oracle are kept
chapter.text: Verses 30 and 31 give variant wordings of the same saying, introduced identically with "and again he saith." The record shows its own transmission working: a prophetic line remembered in more than one form, and preserved that way.

chapter.title: Deliverance is promised without a date
chapter.text: The final verse grants the outcome and withholds the timing: he will deliver, according to his own will and pleasure. Limhi's people will in fact wait years and escape by a stratagem. The chapter is careful not to say when.

chapter.title: Slavery to kin is offered as good news
chapter.text: Verse 15's proposal, better slaves to the Nephites than tributaries to the Lamanites, is made in the same breath as the rejoicing. Nothing in the chapter treats it as shocking. Nothing else in the record conveys what the previous decades had been like so efficiently.

applications.title: Notice what your persistence starts
applications.text: A whole history began because people would not stop asking. Before you press something, consider that you may get it, and that the getting is the beginning rather than the end.

applications.title: Admit the strugglings that were in vain
applications.text: Limhi does not pretend the failed attempts succeeded. Name an effort of yours that did not work, say so plainly, and then ask what an effectual one would look like.

applications.title: Recite the history
applications.text: When you need hope, rehearse specific things God has already done: for Israel, for your family, for you. Limhi's argument is entirely from precedent and he names the instances.

applications.title: Watch for excess of a good motive
applications.text: Zeniff's fault was being over-zealous to inherit what was his fathers'. Identify a good desire you hold strongly enough that it has started costing other people something.

applications.title: Ask who is surprised
applications.text: Limhi's question invites his people to find their own situation unsurprising. Applied honestly to a difficulty of your own, it is uncomfortable and clarifying.

applications.title: Turn, trust, serve, then wait
applications.text: The three conditions are given plainly and the timing is not. Do the three, and accept that the schedule is not part of the promise.

questions.text: Where am I traveling confidently on a route I do not actually know?
What have I accepted as an improvement that would have horrified me a few years ago?
Which of my strugglings have been in vain, and am I willing to say so?
What good thing am I over-zealous about?
Whose warning have I dismissed because of what it would cost me to accept it?
What am I sowing that I would not want to reap?
Can I do the turning without setting a deadline for the deliverance?
